claim: Evolutionary reconstruction algorithms are highly sensitive to their inputs: the sequences used and their alignments.
source: Such algorithms are highly sensitive to their inputs: the sequences used and their alignments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of evolutionary reconstruction algorithms.

claim: The reproducibility of an all-sequence, single-alignment reconstruction, measured by comparing topologies inferred from 90% subsamples, directly correlates with the accuracy of that single-alignment reconstruction.
source: First, the reproducibility of an all-sequence, single-alignment reconstruction, measured by comparing topologies inferred from 90% subsamples, directly correlates with the accuracy of that single-alignment reconstruction, producing a measurable value for something that has been traditionally unknowable.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in the manuscript showing the relationship between precision and accuracy.

claim: Topologies that are most consistent with observations made in the ensemble are more accurate.
source: Second, topologies that are most consistent with the observations made in the ensemble are more accurate and we present a meta algorithm that exploits this property to improve model accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by the ASPEN algorithm results showing improved accuracy compared to all-sequence topologies.

claim: Paralogs tend to perform related, but distinct functions.
source: For protein coding sequences, paralogs tend to perform related, but distinct functions (Prince and Pickett, 2002; Raes and Van de Peer, 2003; Espinosa-Cantú et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reconstructing histories of paralog divergence can aid tremendously in dissecting how functionality is encoded in sequence and structure.
source: Reconstructing histories of paralog divergence can aid tremendously in this endeavor (Thomson et al., 2005; Eick et al., 2012; Rahman et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2015; Daugherty et al., 2016; Harms and Thornton, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The computational complexity of phylogenetic reconstruction scales combinatorially with the number of nodes to be reconstructed.
source: the computational complexity of the problem, which scales combinatorially with the number of nodes to be reconstructed
evidence: This is stated as a known property of phylogenetic reconstruction problems.

claim: Likelihood-based approaches fail to adequately discriminate between topology models when the amount of phylogenetic data is small (<1000 columns).
source: the failure of likelihood-based approaches to adequately discriminate between topology models, especially when the amount of phylogenetic data (number of alignment columns) is small (<1000 columns) (Yang and Zhu, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang and Zhu, 2018.

claim: Phylogenetic reconstruction is sensitive to the input alignment.
source: the sensitivity of phylogenetic reconstruction to the input alignment (Ogden and Rosenberg, 2006; Landan and Graur, 2007; Wong et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011; Blackburne et al., 2013; Sievers et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Joint Bayesian inference of alignment and phylogeny with BAli-Phy is far too computationally expensive to tackle large-scale reconstruction of paralog divergence.
source: The current state-of-the-art in addressing the effect of alignment uncertainty on phylogenetic reconstruction, joint Bayesian inference of alignment and phylogeny with BAli-Phy (Redelings and Suchard, 2005; Suchard and Redelings, 2006), is far too computationally expensive to tackle large-scale reconstruction of paralog divergence.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current methods with citations to the BAli-Phy papers.

claim: 600 protein families were simulated, each containing 15 paralogs represented by 66 orthologs for a total of 990 sequences.
source: We simulated 600 protein families, each containing 15 paralogs represented by 66 orthologs – a total of 990 sequences.
evidence: This describes the simulation setup used in the study.

claim: Subsamples from all simulated orthosets were overwhelmingly monophyletic.
source: We found that subsamples from all our simulated orthosets were overwhelmingly monophyletic, so our selection of ortholog common ancestors as leaves for our reconstruction was justified.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data.

claim: The largest effect on accuracy came from the choice of alignment algorithm.
source: The largest effect on accuracy came from the choice of alignment algorithm, consistent with previous studies (Morrison and Ellis, 1997; Mugridge et al., 2000; Wong et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2011; Blackburne et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis with supporting citations.

claim: L-INS-i alignments produced the most accurate reconstructions.
source: L-INS-i alignments produced the most accurate reconstructions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: FastTree2 and RAxML performed very similarly across all alignment algorithms.
source: FastTree2 and RAxML performed very similarly across all alignment algorithms, also consistent with earlier observations (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with a supporting citation.

claim: Precision directly correlates with accuracy with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.91 and p-value < 1e-100.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, precision directly correlates with accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.91 and p-value < 1e-100)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Precision of reconstruction for the LacI family is 0.698.
source: Precision of reconstruction for the LacI family is 0.698, indicated by a dashed line in Figure 1E
evidence: This is a measured value from the LacI family analysis.

claim: The all-sequence LacI topology is not entirely accurate, in accordance with its rather low reproducibility.
source: suggesting that the reconstruction is of moderate difficulty and that the all-sequence LacI topology is not entirely accurate, in accordance with its rather low reproducibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the precision measurement and the correlation between precision and accuracy.

claim: Topology search reliably identified the better scoring topologies under the substitution model.
source: We found no such cases among our synthetic families (Figure 2A). While it is reassuring that topology search reliably identified the better scoring topologies
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The all-sequence topology scored better both under the substitution model used in phylogenetic inference and under the different model used for simulating sequence evolution.
source: Even more surprising, the all-sequence topology scored better both under the substitution model used in phylogenetic inference and under the different model used for simulating sequence evolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and see Materials and methods for choice of substitution models).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: For high-precision families, the all-sequence topology scores better than the true topology, given the combination of the substitution model used in simulation and the true alignment.
source: In fact, for high-precision families, the all-sequence topology scores better than the true topology, given the combination of the substitution model used in simulation and the true alignment.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: True topologies were always located on a plateau outside of the optimum well on the all-sequence alignment likelihood surface.
source: We were surprised to discover that true topologies were always located on this plateau, outside of the optimum well on the all-sequence alignment likelihood surface (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Alignment accuracy is correlated with topology accuracy with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.80.
source: Alignment accuracy is correlated with topology accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.80)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The correlation between alignment accuracy and topology accuracy is weaker than that between topology precision and accuracy.
source: but this correlation is weaker than that between topology precision and accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.91).
evidence: This is a comparison of two correlation coefficients from the data analysis.

claim: Alignment accuracy and alignment robustness are 97% correlated.
source: Alignment accuracy and alignment robustness are 97% correlated
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Alignment robustness and topology accuracy have a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.78.
source: Alignment robustness and topology accuracy have a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.78, while topology precision and topology accuracy have a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.91.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ASPEN's scoring function rewards incorporation of frequently observed path lengths and penalizes rarely observed ones.
source: This scoring function rewards incorporation of frequently observed path lengths and penalizes rarely observed ones.
evidence: This describes the design of the ASPEN scoring function.

claim: In 90.7% of all families, the top-ranked ASPEN topology is equal to or more accurate than the all-sequence topology.
source: Figure 4A demonstrates that in the vast majority of cases (90.7% of all families) the top-ranked ASPEN topology is equal to or more accurate than the all-sequence topology.
evidence: This is a result from the ASPEN analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ASPEN topology is more accurate than the all-sequence topology for 53.8% of families.
source: The ASPEN topology is more accurate for 53.8% of families.
evidence: This is a result from the ASPEN analysis.

claim: At the highest precision values, the top-ranked ASPEN topology is the true topology.
source: At the highest precision values, where all-sequence topologies are the most accurate, the top-ranked ASPEN topology is the true topology.
evidence: This is an observation from the ASPEN results.

claim: The top-ranked topology is the most accurate for 36.9% of families.
source: The top-ranked topology is also the most accurate for 36.9% of families
evidence: This is a result from the ASPEN analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For 63.1% of families, the most accurate tree is not the top-ranked tree.
source: while for the remaining 63.1% of families the most accurate tree is not the top-ranked tree.
evidence: This is a result from the ASPEN analysis.

claim: 75% of the time the most accurate tree is in the top ten trees returned by ASPEN.
source: However, the most-accurate tree recovered is still related to the topologies likelihood score and 75% of the time the most accurate tree is in the top ten trees returned by ASPEN.
evidence: This is a result from the ASPEN analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For 99% of families, the most accurate among the top 50 topologies returned by ASPEN is better or equal in accuracy to the all-sequence topology.
source: For 99% of families, the most accurate among the top 50 topologies returned by ASPEN is better or equal in accuracy to the all-sequence topology (76% of the time it is better).
evidence: This is a result from the ASPEN analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Among paths on which true and all-sequence topologies disagree, the length consistent with the true topology was observed more frequently than the length consistent with the all-sequence topology for half or more paths across all but the highest-precision bin.
source: Among paths on which the two topologies disagree, the length consistent with the true topology was observed more frequently than the length consistent with the all-sequence topology for half or more paths across all but the highest-precision bin (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the path length analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the highest-precision bin, the true and all-sequence topologies disagree on a very small fraction of path lengths (4.8%).
source: In the highest-precision bin, reconstruction is extremely accurate and the true and all-sequence topologies disagree on a very small fraction of path lengths (4.8%).
evidence: This is an observation from the path length analysis.

claim: The all-sequence LacI topology does not appear among the top 500 ASPEN topologies.
source: The all-sequence LacI topology does not appear among the top 500 ASPEN topologies, having scored significantly worse then the ASPEN trees according to the log-frequency scoring function.
evidence: This is an observation from the LacI analysis.

claim: All 500 ASPEN topologies are more consistent with observations across the ensemble of subsampled LacI topologies than the all-sequence reconstruction.
source: This indicates that all 500 ASPEN topologies are more consistent with observations across the ensemble of subsampled LacI topologies than the all-sequence reconstruction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the scoring results for LacI.

claim: The best ASPEN topology is more accurate than the all-sequence topology for LacI, but none of the reconstructed topologies are likely to match exactly the true divergence of LacI paralogs.
source: Taken together with our findings for synthetic families, these results suggest that the best ASPEN topology is more accurate than the all-sequence topology, but that none of the reconstructed topologies are likely to match exactly the true divergence of LacI paralogs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the LacI results and the synthetic family results.

claim: ASPEN identifies topologies in the face of misleading likelihood landscapes resulting from each individual input alignment, on which the true topology is not the maximum likelihood topology.
source: Crucially, ASPEN identifies these topologies in the face of misleading likelihood landscapes resulting from each individual input alignment, on which the true topology is not the maximum likelihood topology, or even located within the optimum well.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of likelihood landscapes and ASPEN performance.

claim: ASPEN tree accuracy declines as the reconstruction task gets harder, but its decline is significantly slower than that of single all-sequence reconstructions.
source: Finally, we showed that, although ASPEN tree accuracy declines as the reconstruction task gets harder (as evidenced by decreased precision and accuracy of the all-sequence tree), its decline is significantly slower than that of single all-sequence reconstructions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of ASPEN and all-sequence topology accuracies across different precision levels.

claim: ASPEN is able to identify when an all-sequence tree is likely to be inaccurate via precision.
source: Importantly, ASPEN is able to identify when an all-sequence tree is likely to be inaccurate (via precision)
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between precision and accuracy.

claim: Sequence evolution was simulated over synthetic phylogenies using the JTT substitution model.
source: Simulation was carried out over synthetic phylogenies using indel-seq-gen (Strope et al., 2007; Strope et al., 2009; Rambaut and Grass, 1997) under the JTT substitution model.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: The WAG substitution model was deliberately used for topology inference instead of the JTT substitution model used for simulating protein families.
source: The WAG substitution model was deliberately used for topology inference, instead of the JTT substitution model used for simulating protein families, in order to emulate the more realistic scenario where models used for reconstruction of phylogenies for natural families do not precisely match the substitution patterns in those families.
evidence: This describes a deliberate methodological choice to introduce model violation.

claim: Random 15-leaf phylogenies were generated with average branch lengths of 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, and 1.0 – 100 phylogenies each.
source: Random phylogenies were generated with average branch lengths of 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, and 1.0 –100 phylogenies each.
evidence: This describes the simulation setup.

claim: The Ensembl Compara species tree topology containing 66 metazoan species was grafted to each leaf of each random topology to represent ortholog divergence.
source: Next, the Ensembl Compara species tree topology (Herrero et al., 2016) containing 66 metazoan species was grafted to each leaf of each random topology to represent ortholog divergence.
evidence: This describes the simulation setup.

claim: ASPEN is implemented in python 2.7.
source: ASPEN is implemented in python 2.7.
evidence: This describes the implementation of ASPEN.

claim: The ASPEN development repository is publicly available at https://github.com/NaegleLab/ASPEN.
source: The ASPEN development repository is publicly available at https://github.com/NaegleLab/ASPEN (Sloutsky and Naegle, 2019; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/ASPEN).
evidence: This provides information about code availability.

claim: The LacI family collection contains 23 LacI paralogs represented by 22 to 192 orthologs, for a total of 1777 sequences.
source: The final collection contains 23 LacI paralogs represented by 22 to 192 orthologs, for a total of 1777 sequences (Supplementary Material).
evidence: This describes the LacI dataset used in the study.

claim: MAFFT's L-INS-i protocol, ClustalOmega, and Muscle were used for sequence alignment.
source: We used MAFFT's L-INS-i protocol (Katoh and Standley, 2013), ClustalOmega (Sievers et al., 2011), and Muscle (Edgar, 2004) for sequence alignment
evidence: This describes the alignment methods used.

claim: FastTree2 and RAxML were used to infer phylogenies.
source: and FastTree2 (Price et al., 2010) and RAxML (Stamatakis, 2014) to infer phylogenies.
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic inference methods used.

claim: The combination of L-INS-i and FastTree2 was selected for all subsequent phylogeny inferences because FastTree2 is significantly faster than RAxML.
source: Because FastTree2 is significantly faster than RAxML, we selected the fast and accurate combination of L-INS-i and FastTree2 for all subsequent phylogeny inferences.
evidence: This explains the methodological choice based on speed and accuracy considerations.

claim: The least difficult (most accurate) synthetic families were complete within an hour of total CPU time for ASPEN reconstruction.
source: ASPEN's reconstruction is parallelizable across multiple CPUs and we generally observed that the least difficult (most accurate) synthetic families were complete within an hour of total CPU time
evidence: This describes the computational performance of ASPEN.

claim: The most difficult problems could take up to 400 CPU hr for ASPEN reconstruction.
source: whereas the most difficult problems could take up to 400 CPU hr.
evidence: This describes the computational performance of ASPEN.

claim: The vast majority of N-best trees were always identified early in the ASPEN run (within a few hours).
source: However, the vast majority of N-best trees were always identified early in the the run (within a few hours), with the remainder of the run spent almost exclusively rejecting worse topologies.
evidence: This describes the computational behavior of ASPEN.

claim: Orthology and paralogy are two forms of evolutionary homology between genetic sequences introduced by Walter Fitch.
source: Orthology and paralogy are two forms of evolutionary homology between genetic sequences introduced by Walter Fitch (Fitch, 2000; Koonin, 2005)
evidence: This is a historical fact about the terminology with citations.

claim: Homologs diverged through speciation are called orthologs.
source: Homologs diverged through speciation are called orthologs
evidence: This is a definition from established terminology.

claim: Homologs diverged through the duplication of a genomic region are called paralogs.
source: while those diverged through the duplication of a genomic region are called paralogs.
evidence: This is a definition from established terminology.

claim: Reconstructing speciation history from a single protein family is of little interest aside from identifying extremely rare evolutionary events.
source: Reconstructing speciation history from a single protein family is of little interest aside from identifying extremely rare evolutionary events, such as horizontal gene transfer and reciprocal paralog loss, through reconciliation of the protein phylogeny with the accepted species phylogeny (Nakhleh, 2013; Kamneva and Ward, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the biological utility of reconstructing speciation history from single protein families, with citations.

claim: Topologies of yeast divergence reconstructed from single genes, while rarely identical, shared much greater similarity than randomly generated topologies.
source: Inspired by the findings of Salichos and Rokas, who showed that topologies of yeast divergence reconstructed from single genes, while rarely identical, shared much greater similarity than randomly generated topologies (Salichos and Rokas, 2013)
evidence: This is a citation to previous work by Salichos and Rokas.

claim: ASPEN produces significantly more accurate topology models than those produced by a single-alignment reconstruction from all available sequences.
source: Our methodology, ASPEN (Accuracy through Subsampling of Protein EvolutioN), produces significantly more accurate topology models than those produced by a single-alignment reconstruction from all available sequences.
evidence: This is a summary claim about ASPEN's performance based on the results presented.

claim: The test set of simulated families spans a range of difficulty, as observed by a range of inaccuracies across the families.
source: Therefore, our test set of simulated families spans a range of difficulty, as observed by a range of inaccuracies across the families, which allows us to observe the performance of phylogenetic reconstruction as a function of that difficulty.
evidence: This is an inference about the test set based on the observed range of accuracies.

claim: For families with high accuracy, when precision is also high, the difference in log-likelihood between subsampled and all-sequence topologies varied from 0 to 10-4.
source: For families with high accuracy, when precision is also high, the difference varied from 0 to 10-4, suggesting that the all-sequence topology is within the optimum well.
evidence: This is an observation from the log-likelihood analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The degree of optimum displacement due to resampling and realignment, captured by the precision metric, reflects the overall dispersion of plausible topology models around the true topology.
source: We suggest that the degree of optimum displacement due to resampling and realignment, captured by our precision metric, reflects the overall dispersion of plausible topology models around the true topology.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed relationship between precision and likelihood landscapes.

claim: Less accurate all-sequence topologies are inferred over surfaces more susceptible to the perturbation of input sequence selection and alignment.
source: In other words, less accurate all-sequence topologies are inferred over surfaces more susceptible to the perturbation of input sequence selection and alignment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed relationship between accuracy, precision, and likelihood landscapes.

claim: Alignment accuracy is correlated with topology accuracy, but this correlation is weaker than that between topology precision and accuracy.
source: Alignment accuracy is correlated with topology accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.80), but this correlation is weaker than that between topology precision and accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.91).
evidence: This is a comparison of correlation coefficients from the data analysis.

claim: Alignment robustness is almost perfectly correlated with alignment accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.97).
source: We used Guidance2 (Sela et al., 2015) to determine alignment robustness and found that this is almost perfectly correlated with alignment accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.97)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the alignment analysis.

claim: Alignment robustness captures slightly less variance in topology accuracy than alignment accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient between alignment robustness and topology accuracy of 0.78).
source: but captures slightly less variance in topology accuracy (Pearson correlation coefficient between alignment robustness and topology accuracy of 0.78, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the alignment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Precision of topology inference naturally incorporates alignment robustness to perturbations arising from sequence subsampling and the effect of alignment robustness on topology inference.
source: On the other hand, the precision of topology inference naturally incorporates alignment robustness to perturbations arising from sequence subsampling, but also incorporates the effect of alignment robustness (or lack thereof) on topology inference, resulting in a metric that is more highly correlated with topology accuracy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why precision is more correlated with accuracy than alignment robustness.

claim: ASPEN provides greatest improvement over single-alignment inference when precision is below 0.9.
source: ASPEN provides greatest improvement over single-alignment inference when precision is below 0.9, where it is very likely that ASPEN's top topology will be more accurate than the all-sequence topology.
evidence: This is an observation from the ASPEN results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The most accurate topologies are ranked highest by ASPEN.
source: The fast drop-off in rank demonstrates that the most accurate topologies are ranked highest by ASPEN.
evidence: This is an observation from the ranking analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ASPEN's approach and likelihood scoring function, which reflect consistency with ensemble-observed features, are related to topology accuracy.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that ASPEN's approach and likelihood scoring function, which reflect consistency with ensemble-observed features (Equation 1) are related to topology accuracy.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ASPEN results.

claim: For 76% of families, the most accurate among the top 50 topologies returned by ASPEN is better than the all-sequence topology.
source: For 99% of families, the most accurate among the top 50 topologies returned by ASPEN is better or equal in accuracy to the all-sequence topology (76% of the time it is better).
evidence: This is a result from the ASPEN analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: As precision drops, the number of topologies that are more accurate than all-sequence increases.
source: Not surprisingly, for families with highly accurate all-sequence topologies, which also have high precision, one or few topologies are equally or more accurate, which corresponds with the top-ranked ASPEN tree also recovering the true topology. Strikingly, as precision drops, even a small amount, the number of topologies that are more accurate than all-sequence increases.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At the extreme-end where precision is at its lowest observed, all 50 ASPEN topologies are more accurate than the all-sequence topology.
source: At the extreme-end, where precision is at its lowest observed, all 50 ASPEN topologies are more accurate than the all-sequence topology.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The fraction of disagreeing paths for which the ensemble correctly identifies the true length remains surprisingly constant as precision falls.
source: Although the fraction of all paths with incorrect length in the all-sequence topology (overall bar height in Figure 5A) increases dramatically as precision falls, the fraction of disagreeing paths for which the ensemble correctly identifies the true length (fraction of bar filled with blue) remains surprisingly constant.
evidence: This is an observation from the path length analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Log-frequency score differences between ASPEN topologies decrease at lower precision.
source: Accordingly, log-frequency score differences between ASPEN topologies also decrease at lower precision (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), reflecting more uniform confidence in any individual topology.
evidence: This is an observation from the score analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Log-frequency scores decay faster at higher precision.
source: Log-frequency scores decay faster at higher precision (Figure 6), reflecting a greater difference in confidence for each lower ranked topology, as previously discussed.
evidence: This is an observation from the score analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The top ASPEN topology incorporates the [Mal-B, AscG, GalRS] common ancestor, which appears in an additional 46% of ASPEN topologies.
source: While the top ASPEN topology incorporates the [Mal-B, AscG, GalRS] common ancestor, which appears in and additional 46% of ASPEN topologies
evidence: This is an observation from the LacI topology analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Alternative placement of the Mal-B terminal branch in the all-sequence topology produces a different ancestral node, which appears in only 24% of ASPEN topologies.
source: alternative placement of the Mal-B terminal branch in the all-sequence topology produces a different ancestral node, which appears in only 24% of ASPEN topologies.
evidence: This is an observation from the LacI topology analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The all-sequence topology is missing the [CscR, IdnR, GntR] common ancestor, which appears in 76% of ASPEN topologies.
source: Worse, the all-sequence topology is missing the [CscR, IdnR, GntR] common ancestor, which appears in 76% of ASPEN topologies
evidence: This is an observation from the LacI topology analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The all-sequence topology incorporates the [IdnR, GntR, ExuR, KdgR, FruR, ScrR-BD, TreR] common ancestor, which appears in only 6% of ASPEN topologies.
source: incorporating instead the [IdnR, GntR, ExuR, KdgR, FruR, ScrR-BD, TreR] common ancestor, which appears in only 6% of ASPEN topologies.
evidence: This is an observation from the LacI topology analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Downstream analyses would do well to reflect uncertainty by considering multiple likely topologies produced by ASPEN.
source: In lieu of using a single topology, downstream analyses would do well to reflect this uncertainty by considering multiple likely topologies produced by ASPEN.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings about topological uncertainty.

claim: The sequence resampling approach treats sequence alignment and phylogeny reconstruction as a single inference procedure subject to multiple sources of uncertainty.
source: On the other hand, the sequence resampling approach we presented occurs farther upstream in the inference process, treating sequence alignment and phylogeny reconstruction as a single inference procedure subject to multiple sources of uncertainty.
evidence: This describes the conceptual approach of ASPEN.

claim: The phylogenetic bootstrap cannot address the reliability of the individual sites (alignment positions) it resamples.
source: The traditional method of assessing the reliability of phylogenetic reconstruction, the phylogenetic bootstrap (Felsenstein, 1985), cannot address the reliability of the individual sites (alignment positions) it resamples.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the phylogenetic bootstrap with a citation.

claim: For most protein families, it will be necessary to consider multiple equally likely models of evolutionary divergence.
source: Specifically, we propose that for most protein families, it will be necessary to consider multiple equally likely models of evolutionary divergence.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings about topological uncertainty.

claim: Divergence reconstructions for well-studied protein domain families are relied upon extensively by the scientific community.
source: Divergence reconstructions for well-studied protein domain families are relied upon extensively by the scientific community.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of phylogenetic reconstructions in the field.

claim: The human kinome was constructed just from human sequences and has been cited over 6000 times to date.
source: For example the human kinome, which has been cited over 6000 times to date, was constructed just from human sequences – an example of extreme subsampling, with each ancestor represented by a single sequence.
evidence: This is a statement about a specific published phylogeny and its citation count.

claim: Topology reconstructions from single alignments with sparse subsampling are likely to be extremely inaccurate.
source: Topology reconstructions from single alignments with sparse subsampling are likely to be extremely inaccurate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about the relationship between subsampling and accuracy.

claim: Individual reconstructions are extremely unreliable, even for relatively high-precision families, with very few descendants representing each ancestor.
source: We found individual reconstructions are extremely unreliable, even for relatively high-precision families, with very few descendants representing each ancestor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings from the simulation study.

claim: Revisiting important protein domains using ASPEN's approach is worthwhile.
source: These observations suggest that revisiting these important protein domains using ASPEN's approach, including quantifying the likely accuracy of published trees and constructing and ranking trees most consistent with the available homolog sequences, is worthwhile.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings about the inaccuracy of single-alignment reconstructions.

claim: Accuracy of phylogenetic inference in general appears to be affected in a sequence length-dependent manner by site non-independence.
source: Accuracy of phylogenetic inference in general appears to be affected in a sequence length-dependent manner, with site non-independence resulting in less phylogenetic signal than site-independent sequences of the same length (Nasrallah et al., 2011; Huelsenbeck and Nielsen, 1999).
evidence: This is a statement about the effects of site non-independence with citations.

claim: If reduction in phylogenetic signal is the principal effect of non-independent evolution of sites, then precision should diminish accordingly, and the strength of the accuracy-precision relationship should not be affected.
source: If reduction in phylogenetic signal is indeed the principal effect of non-independent evolution of sites, then precision should diminish accordingly, and the strength of the accuracy-precision relationship should not be affected.
evidence: This is a speculation about how site non-independence might affect the accuracy-precision relationship.

claim: Identifying evolutionary circumstances which result in systematic breakdown of the accuracy-precision relationship is vitally important for future work.
source: Identifying evolutionary circumstances which result in such systematic breakdown of the accuracy-precision relationship is vitally important for future work.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: ASPEN analysis of any real protein family starts with selecting the ancestral nodes for search space decomposition.
source: ASPEN analysis of any real protein family starts with selecting the ancestral nodes for search space decomposition.
evidence: This describes the first step in applying ASPEN to real data.

claim: The only requirement for ancestral node selection is sufficient confidence in each ancestor's existence, as evidenced by robust inference over any set of reasonable input alignments or alignment perturbations.
source: The only requirement is sufficient confidence in each ancestor's existence, as evidenced by robust inference over any set of reasonable input alignments or alignment perturbations.
evidence: This describes the criterion for selecting ancestral nodes for ASPEN analysis.

claim: ASPEN methodology can be used recursively to separately reconstruct the divergence of closely related paralogs.
source: ASPEN methodology can be used recursively to separately reconstruct the divergence of these paralogs – another advantage of decomposing the search space at high confidence nodes.
evidence: This describes a potential application of ASPEN.

claim: Applicability of ASPEN analysis to any particular family hinges on the existence of high confidence ancestors and the willingness to sacrifice reconstruction of clades below those ancestors.
source: Clearly, applicability of ASPEN analysis to any particular family hinges on the existence of such high confidence ancestors and the willingness to sacrifice reconstruction of clades below those ancestors.
evidence: This describes the requirements for applying ASPEN.

claim: ASPEN analysis remains applicable given at least one integrated out clade, although the usefulness of that analysis is expected to diminish as more leaf sequences fall outside of such clades.
source: ASPEN analysis remains applicable given at least one integrated out clade, although we expect the usefulness of that analysis to diminish as more leaf sequences fall outside of such clades.
evidence: This describes the limitations of ASPEN applicability.

claim: ASPEN's branch-and-bound algorithm provides a powerful guarantee of completeness that the N-best trees were produced at the end of its run.
source: ASPEN's branch-and-bound algorithm provides a powerful guarantee of completeness – that the N-best trees were produced – at the end of its run
evidence: This describes a property of the ASPEN algorithm.

claim: Execution times and resource requirements can be substantial for large families using ASPEN.
source: but execution times and resource requirements can be substantial for large families.
evidence: This describes a limitation of ASPEN.

claim: Topology assembly can be truncated after a fraction of the full run time, retaining a nearly-complete collection of N-best trees.
source: Dispensing with the branch-and-bound guarantee, topology assembly can be truncated after a fraction, sometimes a very small fraction, of the full run time, retaining a nearly-complete collection of N-best trees.
evidence: This describes a practical approach to reducing ASPEN runtime.

claim: For common ancestors of orthologs, the species divergence topology should be used for the divergence of orthologs, unless truly compelling evidence to the contrary exists.
source: For common ancestors of orthologs, we strongly recommend using the species divergence topology for the divergence of orthologs, unless truly compelling evidence to the contrary exists.
evidence: This is a recommendation for downstream analysis after ASPEN reconstruction.

claim: The correct speciation topology was never recovered for all 15 paralogs in the simulated families.
source: In our analysis of simulated families, where ortholog evolution was simulated over the same species tree in each case, the correct speciation topology was never recovered for all 15 paralogs, underscoring the futility of reconstructing species divergence from single protein families.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation study.

claim: All of the large phylogenetic reconstructions required to build a topology ensemble can be carried out concurrently, allowing ASPEN to take maximal advantage of high-performance computing resources.
source: Unlike in simultaneous alignment and phylogeny inference, all of the large phylogenetic reconstructions required to build a topology ensemble can be carried out concurrently, allowing ASPEN to take maximal advantage of high-performance computing resources.
evidence: This describes an advantage of ASPEN's approach.

claim: ASPEN's topology reconstruction algorithm is not affected by the number of leaf sequences within integrated-out clades, only by the number of such clades.
source: ASPEN's topology reconstruction algorithm itself is not affected by the number of leaf sequences within integrated-out clades, only by the number of such clades, making it scale much better with the total number of input sequences than simultaneous co-estimation approaches.
evidence: This describes a scalability advantage of ASPEN.

claim: ASPEN as a meta analysis approach is likely to continue to boost the accuracy of individual alignment and tree reconstruction approaches, regardless of the specific underlying algorithms.
source: We anticipate that, as a meta analysis approach to tree evaluation and reconstruction, ASPEN is likely to continue to boost the accuracy of individual alignment and tree reconstruction approaches, regardless of the specific underlying alignment and reconstruction algorithms or the application (e.g. whether it is subsampling from orthologs to infer paralog relationships or subsampling from genomes to reconstruct species relationships).
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of ASPEN.

claim: The current implementation of ASPEN as a subsampling and scoring approach is immediately tractable for nearly all protein families.
source: The current implementation of ASPEN as a subsampling and scoring approach is immediately tractable for nearly all protein families.
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of ASPEN.

claim: ASPEN's branch-and-bound reconstruction algorithm is immediately tractable for reasonably sized families, such as the LacI family.
source: ASPEN's branch-and-bound reconstruction algorithm is also immediately tractable for reasonably sized families, such as the LacI family.
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of ASPEN's reconstruction algorithm.

claim: The sequence subsampling approach, the path-length frequency distributions it provides, and the log-frequency scoring function scale with the number of integrated out clades much better than the branch-and-bound algorithm.
source: However, the sequence subsampling approach, the path-length frequency distributions it provides, and the log-frequency scoring function are powerful tools in their own right, which scale with the number of integrated out clades much better than the branch-and-bound algorithm.
evidence: This describes the scalability of different components of ASPEN.

claim: A more efficient search of topology space under the log-frequency scoring function, with a guarantee and/or estimation of completeness, is possible.
source: A more efficient search of topology space under this objective function, with a guarantee and/or estimation of completeness, is possible.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements to ASPEN.

claim: It may be possible to structure subsampling so that the resulting frequency distributions are even more reflective of the true topology.
source: It may be possible to structure subsampling so that the resulting frequency distributions are even more reflective of the true topology.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential improvements to ASPEN.

claim: A mechanism for robust inference of branch lengths for ASPEN-constructed topologies that integrates over the uncertainty of alignment and reconstruction below selected ancestors is clearly desirable.
source: Finally, a mechanism for robust inference of branch lengths for ASPEN-constructed topologies that, similar to ASPEN topology reconstruction, integrates over the uncertainty of alignment and reconstruction below selected ancestors, is clearly desirable.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed to extend ASPEN.

claim: Phylogenetic inference is an extremely difficult problem, particularly for individual protein families, where short amino acid sequences contain limited phylogenetic signal.
source: Phylogenetic inference is an extremely difficult problem, particularly for individual protein families, where short amino acid sequences contain limited phylogenetic signal.
evidence: This is a statement about the difficulty of phylogenetic inference.

claim: The sensitivity of inference and alignment algorithms to their inputs is a result of the failure of objective functions to accurately model the mutational events that underlie the divergence nodes in an evolutionary tree.
source: Here, we demonstrated that the sensitivity of inference and alignment algorithms to their inputs is a result of the failure of objective functions to accurately model the mutational events that underlie the divergence nodes in an evolutionary tree, which manifest in both alignment and inference procedures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of likelihood landscapes.

claim: Integrating across a lot of models that are wrong in different ways, but right in the same way, yields more useful models of evolutionary divergence.
source: Extending this, we propose that integrating across a lot of models that are wrong in different ways, but right in the same way, yields more useful models of evolutionary divergence.
evidence: This is a philosophical statement about the ASPEN approach.

claim: Topologies capturing more of the shared information across many incorrect models are significantly more accurate.
source: This is based on the observation that topologies capturing more of the shared information across many incorrect models are significantly more accurate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ASPEN results.

claim: For especially difficult inference problems, it is important to consider multiple models as equally viable explanations of evolutionary history.
source: However, we also find that, for especially difficult inference problems (where all-sequence topologies are imprecise, that is have low reproducibility under subsampling) it is important to consider multiple models as equally viable explanations of evolutionary history.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings about topological uncertainty.

claim: For most real evolutionary inference problems, scientists should integrate their analyses over multiple plausible phylogenetic models.
source: In other words, for most real evolutionary inference problems, scientists should integrate their analyses over multiple plausible phylogenetic models.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings.

claim: The methodology facilitates both an overall assessment of accuracy of topology reconstruction for any particular problem, and reconstruction of an appropriate number of maximally plausible topological models.
source: The methodology we presented facilitates both an overall assessment of accuracy of topology reconstruction for any particular problem, and, in light of that assessment, reconstruction of an appropriate number of maximally plausible topological models.
evidence: This is a summary of what ASPEN provides.

claim: ASPEN is geared toward analysis of precisely the most difficult class ancestors: ancient ancestors of multiple paralogs.
source: Crucially, ASPEN is geared toward analysis of precisely the most difficult class ancestors: ancient ancestors of multiple paralogs.
evidence: This describes the target application of ASPEN.

claim: Individual ancestral nodes can vary dramatically in their difficulty of inference.
source: It should be noted that individual ancestral nodes can vary dramatically in their difficulty of inference
evidence: This is a statement about the variability in inference difficulty.

claim: Many ancestors of great biological interest can be inferred with very high accuracy, despite low overall accuracy of topology inference for that family.
source: and many ancestors of great biological interest can be inferred with very high accuracy, despite low overall accuracy of topology inference for that family.
evidence: This is a statement about the possibility of accurate inference of specific ancestors.

claim: Given high confidence in the existence of an ancestor, reconstruction of that ancestor's sequence is robust with respect to topological uncertainty for the clade below it.
source: Moreover, given high confidence in the existence of such an ancestor, reconstruction of that ancestor's sequence is robust with respect to topological uncertainty for the clade below it (Eick et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement with a citation to Eick et al., 2017.

claim: A critical step in evolutionary analysis is to determine which inferred ancestors are reliable and which are not.
source: A critical step in evolutionary analysis, then, is to determine which inferred ancestors are reliable – both with respect to systematic biases and with respect to uncertainty due to various sources of random noise – and which are not.
evidence: This is a statement about best practices in evolutionary analysis.

claim: ASPEN topologies can be used to evaluate consistency of an ancestor's inference across the most likely topologies, similar to the traditional phylogenetic bootstrap.
source: ASPEN topologies can be used for this purpose in a fashion similar to the traditional phylogenetic bootstrap, with the additional benefit of evaluating consistency of an ancestor's inference across the most likely topologies.
evidence: This describes a potential use of ASPEN topologies.
